title: Unjust accusations: Leipzig and Cassel left Reformed grace standing; no illusory will toward the reprobate
pass_a_gloss: Unjust accusations against the Reformed. The dissent of the Reformers as to Universal Grace, Redemption, Vocation, the Saxons in the Leipzig Colloquy of the year 1631 had not pressed. The Rinteln men in the Cassel Colloquy (as seen above) confessed that the foundation of divine Grace stands unshaken through the Reformed, and that both sides agree, 1. In equally damning Pelagian & Semi-Pelagian dogmas. 2. In pressing practical rules which suspend salvation & Justification — this [Justification] from antecedent faith, that [salvation] also from perseverance. And certainly it was imposed on the Reformed, as if they had asserted any illusory will in God with respect to the reprobate — which will is always serious, both as to the exacting of duty in the Word; and as to the proposing of the one way to salvation, through faith in Christ; and as to the truth of that individual nexus between faith & salvation; on which is founded the perpetual truth of that saying, whoever will have believed will be saved, &c. On which matter in the Controversy with the early Arminians IV. thereafter & Controv. XXXI. & we in the Biblical Vindication at the place Matthew 11:28.
pass_b_english: Unjust accusations against the Reformed. As for the Reformers' dissent on universal grace, redemption, and vocation: the Saxons at the Leipzig Colloquy of 1631 did not press it. The Rinteln theologians at the Cassel Colloquy (as already seen above) confessed that the foundation of divine grace stands unshaken among the Reformed, and that both sides agree (1) in equally condemning Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian dogmas, and (2) in pressing the practical rules that suspend justification on antecedent faith, and salvation also on perseverance.

And it was certainly laid on the Reformed as if they had asserted some illusory will in God toward the reprobate — whereas that will is always serious: as to the exacting of duty in the Word; as to the proposing of the one way to salvation, through faith in Christ; and as to the truth of that individual bond between faith and salvation. On these the perpetual truth of the saying rests: whoever believes will be saved, and so on.
On this see the Controversy with the early Arminians, IV, and afterward Controv. XXXI; and our own Biblical Vindication at Matthew 11:28.
source_text: Iniqua accusationes in Reformat. Dissensionem Reformatorum, quoad Universalem Gratiam, Redemptionem, Vocationem, non urserant Saxonici in Colloquio Lipsiensi, Anni 1631. Rintelenses in Colloquio Cassellano (ut visum supra) fassi sunt, inconcussum esse per Reformatos, Gratiae divinae fundamentum, & convenire inter utrosque, 1. In damnandis ex aequo Pelagianis & Semi-Pelagianis dogmatis. 2. In urgendis regulis practicis, quae salutem & Justificationem suspendunt, hanc ab antecedente fide, illam etiam à perseverantia. Et certè impositum Reformatis fuit, quasi voluntatem ullam in Deo asseruerint illusoriam, respectu reproborum, quae semper seria, tùm quoad exactionem officii in Verbo; tùm, quoad propositionem unice ad salutem viae, per fidem in Christum; tum quoad veritatem individui illius nexûs, inter fidem & salutem; In quibus fundatur perpetua veritas illius effati, quicunque crediderit servabitur, &c. Quâ de re in Controv. cum primis Armin. IV. deinceps & Controv. XXXI. & nos in Vind. Bibl. ad locum Matth. XI. 28.

bible_refs.note: Vind. Bibl. ad locum Matth. XI. 28

choices.why: Charge that God's will toward reprobates is a mere show; Strimesius denies it

choices.english: justification from antecedent faith; salvation also from perseverance
choices.why: hanc tracks Justificationem; illam tracks salutem in the Latin order
